newsitem.title: UK: Hebron deal shows U.S. role despite EU ambition.
newsitem.headline: Hebron deal shows U.S. role despite EU ambition.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent

The deal between Israel and the Palestinians on Hebron has underlined the key role of the United States in the Middle East peace process, despite growing European diplomatic aspirations in the region.

The long-delayed accord which provides for an Israeli withdrawal from much of the West Bank town was finally secured on Wednesday after U.S. envoy Dennis Ross had spent weeks nudging the two sides towards compromise.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher and President Bill Clinton were also deeply involved. Christopher lost no time in securing credit, saying the U.S. role was "essential in helping Israelis and Palestinians achieve their goals".
It was a clear reminder to Europeans that Washington holds most of the cards when it comes to dealing with the Middle East.

The Palestinians and Arab countries have been pushing for a greater European role, to counter what they see as Washington's pro-Israeli stance, and France has spearheaded efforts to raise the profile of the 15-nation European Union, the world's chief provider of aid and trade to the region.

Paris said on Wednesday the EU had played a role in brokering the Hebron deal and would be involved in its implementation through the bloc's special envoy on the Middle East, Spanish diplomat Miguel Angel Moratinos.

But analysts say Hebron showed the continuing necessity of engaging Washington's diplomatic power in a crisis, particularly since Israel is deeply reluctant to accept mediation from any country other than its closest ally.

"The Americans have been willing to use the Europeans sometimes as a way of making the Israelis moderate their demands," said Ibrahim Karawan, head of the Middle East programme at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) in London.
"But as long as Israel opposes an active role by the Europeans and insists on the Americans as sole brokers, then those betting on a European role will be disappointed."

Ailie Saunders of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI) said European policy had, in the last few months, become more effective in putting public pressure on Israel's right-wing government to honour previous agreements with the Palestinians.
"The Europeans have been able to exert more influence, but the only people who can deliver are the Americans," she said.
The United States, with a strong pro-Israel lobby at home, considers the Jewish state to be a key ally.
Although the Palestinians and Arab countries accuse Washington of bias in its efforts to broker peace, they are also aware of weaknesses in the European position.
The chief problem for the EU is that the member states have different views, a problem that has plagued the bloc in its efforts to build a common foreign policy in many areas.

France has taken a more pro-Arab stance, in line with Gaullist tradition, and Britain has been increasingly critical of Israel's actions. But Germany, the Netherlands and some others are much more reluctant to put pressure on Israel.
"There is no common European policy, there are common European slogans," said Karawan. "A greater European role may be a legitimate aspiration but it does not correspond to reality."

The EU has tried to remedy this, by appointing Moratinos as special envoy to the Middle East late last year. But the Spaniard has said he will not push French demands for an EU seat at peace talks and outlined a more modest European role.
French President Jacques Chirac toured the Middle East last October and caused uproar in Israel by taking what the Jewish state considered to be a provocative, pro-Arab stance.
A British proposal last year to build a Middle East forum for discussing security has sunk more or less without trace.
Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said last week the United States and Israel were ready to drop their opposition to a bigger EU role.
But European diplomats say they are sceptical about concrete results when there are major crises in the Middle East.

They point not only to the dispute over Hebron but to a row last April, when the United States, Russia and European countries all sent envoys to try and arrange a ceasefire between Israel and Hizbollah guerrillas in southern Lebanon.
The United States did not disguise its irritation with other countries, which Washington felt were interfering with delicate negotiations best left to the world's only remaining superpower.
